Parking on the more suburban sites generally is clustered at the center of the housing groups, in order to separate vehicular traffic from pedestrian traffic.
h) Acoustical Environment: The site planners considered the acoustical environment in their site investigations. Two sites were found to have potential problems and are receiving special attention. The Memphis site is adjacent to major roadways, one of which carries extensive amounts of heavy truck traffic. Measurements of the acoustical environment indicated that this site did not comply with HUD Circular 1396.2, "Noise Abatement and Control: Departmental Policy, Implementation Responsibilities, and Standards." The design solution was to construct an earth berm of sufficient size to shield the site from direct acoustical radiation, and shaped to reflect this radiation upward, and to plan the rest of the site to minimize acoustical impact on the housing units. In this way, the designers were able to create an acceptable environment at this well-located central city site.
At Jersey City particular care is being taken to minimize acoustical pollution from the total energy system.
i) Foundation Designs: The site proposal evaluation team included a senior soils engineer, and his findings were part of the information considered in site selection. Each of the site planners obtained specific subgrade data which was provided to the systems producers for their information. Foundation conditions at the Macon, Memphis, King County and Jersey City sites were found to present potential problems. At Jersey City, an underlying rock strata showed a change in elevation which imposed special design requirements on one system. In Memphis, and St. Louis, where the sites are in urban renewal areas, a number of the housing systems, and the Memphis pedestrian mall, required pile foundations. Pile foundations were used under most high-rise buildings.
At Macon, the planner determined that a number of springs created considerable instability in the soil system on parts of the site, and a thermal mapping technique was used to identify these areas of instability. These areas, consisting generally of alluvial material, have been designated as open spaces, and no housing will be built on or near them.
j) Special Site Features: As noted earlier, environmental considerations in site planning were similar in the planning and design of all of the prototype sites.
